title: 2  Preface
text:
2.1 Setting the Stage
The following work was done with the support of Dr. Mario Bañuelos and Bethany Hernandez-Torres. In particular, this project was originally thought up by Dr. Bañuelos as a series of workshops to support students attending their first REU in data science. The goal was to give students in the workshops the skills to use Google Colab to visualize data, apply statistical methods to draw inferences about the data, and develop background knowledge of the different kinds of machine learning models.
Bethany then brought this project to life, creating both its name, Statistical Analysis, Visualization & Inference (SAVI), and logo for this project. She, alongside Dr. Bañuelos, continues to provide feedback on all aspects of the project from topic choice to the finer details of the code.
SAVI remains as a continuing project to support future students and those willing to learn.
The name for this work was inspired by the word “savi,” which means rain in Mixteco, or Tu’un Sávi (“language of the rain”). Mixteco is one of the most widely spoken indigenous languages in Mexico, primarily in the state of Oaxaca, as well as in Guerrero, Puebla, and among migrant communities in the U.S [1].
In general, data analysis is about making inferences about some set of data through visualizations, statitical models, and mathematical methoods. Here we devlope each of these skills through generalizing examples seen in the following Google Colab notebooks.
We start by first observing what our data looks like through histograms, plots, and time-series charts. Next we consider the statistical methods used to make inferenecs about our data. Then lastly, we apply models our data using methods such as linear regression.

3.4 1. Importing data
In practice, you will normally import data from a file given to you.
Hence, importing data typically require two things. 1. You know the command to load in the data 2. You know both the file path and filename.
Then, if you continue to use google colab for your projects. You can give access google colab access to your google drive, and load files through google drive. Although we will not be utilizing this here. The code for mounting your google drive is below.

# Code for "mounting" (giving google colab access to) google drive
# We will not be using this, but is good to know
#from google.colab import drive
#drive.mount('/content/drive')

Once you have access to data through a CSV or an excel file, to load in data from either file types, we will use the following pandas functions:

pd.read_csv(‘/filepath/file_name.csv’)


pd.read_excel(‘/filepath/file_name.xlsx’)

We will then associate each of these sets of data with a data frame ( in code we denote “df” ).

text:
5.5 Gradient Descent Visual

# -----------------------------
# Generate data
# -----------------------------
np.random.seed(0)
x = np.linspace(0, 10, 30)
true_b = 4.0
true_m = 2.5
y = true_b + true_m * x + np.random.randn(len(x)) * 2

# -----------------------------
# Fix intercept and optimize only slope
# -----------------------------
b_fixed = 4.0

def mse(m, b, x, y):
    return np.mean((b + m * x - y) ** 2)

def grad_m(m, b, x, y):
    n = len(x)
    return (2 / n) * np.sum((b + m * x - y) * x)

# -----------------------------
# Gradient descent on m only
# -----------------------------
m = 0.0
learning_rate = 0.01
num_steps = 12

m_history = [m]
mse_history = [mse(m, b_fixed, x, y)]

for _ in range(num_steps):
    m = m - learning_rate * grad_m(m, b_fixed, x, y)
    m_history.append(m)
    mse_history.append(mse(m, b_fixed, x, y))

# -----------------------------
# Smooth MSE curve
# -----------------------------
m_vals = np.linspace(-0.5, 5.0, 400)
mse_vals = [mse(mv, b_fixed, x, y) for mv in m_vals]

# -----------------------------
# Plot
# -----------------------------
plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6))
plt.plot(m_vals, mse_vals, label="MSE as a function of slope m")
plt.plot(m_history, mse_history, 'o-', label="Gradient descent steps")

# Number each step
for i, (m_i, j_i) in enumerate(zip(m_history, mse_history)):
    plt.text(m_i, j_i, str(i), fontsize=9, ha='right', va='bottom')

# Draw arrows between steps
for i in range(len(m_history) - 1):
    plt.annotate(
        "",
        xy=(m_history[i + 1], mse_history[i + 1]),
        xytext=(m_history[i], mse_history[i]),
        arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", lw=1.2)
    )

plt.xlabel("Slope m")
plt.ylabel("Mean Squared Error")
plt.title(f"MSE vs. Slope with Gradient Descent Steps (b fixed at {b_fixed})")
plt.legend()
plt.grid(True)
plt.show()

# Print step-by-step values
for i in range(len(m_history)):
    print(f"Step {i:2d}: m = {m_history[i]:.4f}, MSE = {mse_history[i]:.4f}")
